doc.title: Eddie Alley interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Potrero district: the only black family and no early sense of segregation
summary: His family was the only black family in Potrero and got along perfectly; he met segregation only after high school looking for work.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Well I was raised in the Potrero district when I was a little kid. And in those days my family was the only black family in the Potrero district, and we didn’t know the difference. I mean we got along perfectly out there. Perfect. Wonderful. In fact the lady upstairs visited us, Mrs. Salmon, and my mother had work to take care of her. She was a white lady, a Scotch lady I think, and it was beautiful. I knew nothing about segregation or nothing like that.

And when I went to grammar school why I’m the one that usually stood on the platform and say, “I pledge allegiance to the flag” to all the kids, when I was in grammar school. So I never came in contact with any segregation until I got out of high school, looking for a job. That’s when the problem came.
